---
title: "Words understood and spoken"
abstract: "In children with Down syndrome, words understood consistently exceed words spoken throughout development — comprehension leads production. Matching on the number of words understood, typically-developing children say a larger fraction of what they understand than children with Down syndrome over the upper part of the comprehension range the data cover; at the lowest comprehension levels the two populations are indistinguishable. Typically-developing comprehension data stop at about 200 understood words, so the contrast is not estimated beyond that."

Every joint model in this report writes spoken vocabulary as a fraction of understood vocabulary, $p_S(a) = p_U(a)\,q(a)$, where $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understand})$ is the **production ratio** — the share of understood words a child also says. The comprehension–production gap is exactly $q(a) < 1$: the smaller $q$, the more a child understands relative to what they say.

## Comprehension leads production in Down syndrome

Across the Down syndrome age range the production ratio stays well below 1 and rises with age (@fig-ds-q): children understand many more words than they say, and the gap narrows only gradually as they get older. The posterior median and 89% interval of $q(a)$ by age:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ds-q
#| echo: false
_qds = load_summary("VG10", "posterior_summary_q")
_qds
```

![Production ratio $q(a) = P(\text{speak}\mid\text{understand})$ for children with Down syndrome (VG10). $q(a) < 1$ throughout — comprehension leads production — rising with age.](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/production_rate.png){#fig-ds-q}

This reproduces, in a large pooled sample, the long-standing observation that expressive vocabulary lags behind receptive vocabulary in Down syndrome.

## Down syndrome vs typically developing: the gap is larger in Down syndrome

Down syndrome and typically-developing children grow vocabulary on very different timescales, so contrasting the gap **by age** would conflate that timescale difference. Instead we match on **comprehension level**: for a child who understands $N$ words, what fraction $q(U = N)$ do they say, in each population? Because words understood and words spoken are coupled per posterior draw within each joint model (Down syndrome from VG10; typically-developing from the young-window model VG13), this is a within-draw contrast at matched comprehension.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ds-td-q
#| echo: false
_facts = dq_facts()
_tab = None
if _facts is not None:
    _tab = _facts["table"][
        ["words", "q_TD_median", "q_DS_median", "dq_median", "dq_ci_lo", "dq_ci_hi", "dq_p_gt0"]
    ].round(3)
    _tab.columns = [
        "Words understood", "TD q", "DS q", "Δq (TD−DS)", "89% lo", "89% hi", "P(TD>DS)"
    ]
    _tab = _tab.reset_index(drop=True)
show_or_pending(_tab, "the matched-comprehension contrast")
```

The difference $\\Delta q = q_{{\\text{{TD}}}} - q_{{\\text{{DS}}}}$ is credibly positive, in the sense of an 89% interval excluding zero, from {dq_words("positive")} understood words, and is largest at {dq_peak()} (@fig-dq). Below that the interval includes zero, and at the bottom of the covered range the point estimate is slightly *negative* ($\\Delta q$ = {dq_at(30)} at 30 understood words), so the two populations are not distinguishable there.

The typically-developing advantage therefore **{dq_trend()}** across the covered comprehension range rather than narrowing: it is absent at low comprehension and largest at the top of the range the typically-developing data support. Because typically-developing comprehension coverage ends at about 200 understood words, the contrast is not estimated beyond that, and these data support no claim either way about whether the gap converges at higher vocabulary levels.

## Limitations

- **Sampling-energy caveat on the typically-developing side.** Both fits are reporting quality and clear the R-hat and effective-sample-size gate, but the typically-developing model (VG13) carries an energy-BFMI caveat below 0.3 (see its convergence banner). Low BFMI indicates the sampler explored the posterior's tails poorly, which bears on the interval bounds quoted here more than on the point estimates.
- **Comprehension coverage.** Typically-developing comprehension+production data span only ~8–18 months (words understood up to ~200); above ~200 understood words the typically-developing estimate is coverage-limited, so the contrast is shown only where both populations reach that comprehension level (coverage ≥ 80%). The upper end of the reported range is therefore the edge of the typically-developing data, not a point at which the contrast was found to stop.
- **Composition, not only propensity.** Matching on the *number* of words understood does not match *which* words. Vocabulary items differ sharply in difficulty, so part of any $q$ difference at matched $N$ reflects the difficulty composition of the words each population knows at that level rather than production propensity alone.
- **Across-model contrast.** Down syndrome (VG10) and typically-developing (VG13) are separate fits on the common 810-item scale. A single joint Down syndrome–typically-developing model would give a formal within-model contrast, but only over this same comprehension range; it is noted as a natural refinement rather than built here.
